summary: Describes a formal framework for Kerberos pre-authentication, the facility that lets a client prove its identity before the key distribution center replies. It models what state is carried and how mechanisms can be combined. It updates RFC 4120 and is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Before a guard hands you a key, you answer a question to show it is you. This defines a tidy way to build those questions and combine them.

questions: what is an armor key in kerberos
subtitle: A common model, a cookie for state and an encrypted tunnel (FAST) for building Kerberos pre-authentication.

tldr.problem: Kerberos treats pre-authentication data as an opaque typed hole, so every mechanism had to invent its own rules for state, for combining with other mechanisms and for protecting its messages. Password-based Kerberos is also open to offline dictionary attacks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a model of the state a mechanism changes, four facilities mechanisms can provide, a cookie and authentication sets for multi-step conversations, and FAST, an armored channel between client and KDC that carries pre-authentication factors.
tldr.outcome: New mechanisms are expected to be built as FAST factors. Conforming implementations must support FAST, the ticket-based armor type and the encrypted challenge factor. The RFC updates RFC 4120.

today: RFC 6113 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 4120, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to the metadata for this page. It remains the definition of the pre-authentication framework and FAST.

sections.title: Why a Framework Was Needed
sections.content:
The core Kerberos specification, RFC 4120, treats pre-authentication data (padata) as an opaque typed hole in messages to the key distribution center (KDC). That freedom was useful, but it made new mechanisms hard to design: each one had to say how it interacts with the others, and common tasks such as strengthening a key or proving identity were redone every time.

This document supplies a framework: the common functions pre-authentication mechanisms perform, how they affect the state of the request and reply, and shared tools. Unlike RFC 3961, the framework is not complete, but mechanism designers are encouraged to follow it and implementations are likely to use plug-in architectures built around it. It also makes it easier to combine several mechanisms, each an authentication factor, into one multi-factor mechanism.

One tool stands out: the flexible authentication secure tunneling padata type, FAST. A mechanism carried inside FAST is called a FAST factor, and the RFC says designers should create FAST factors rather than new mechanisms outside FAST.

The RFC should be read after RFC 3961 and RFC 4120. A conversation is all the authentication messages exchanged between the client and its Authentication Service (AS). It updates RFC 4120.
sections.eli5: Everyone used to make up their own secret handshake for proving who they were, and the handshakes did not fit together. This RFC writes down common rules and a safe tube for handshakes.

sections.title: The Pre-Authentication Model and Its State
sections.content:
A client asks for a ticket with an initial AS request. If pre-authentication is required but missing, the KDC answers KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED. A client that already knows what to use may skip that round trip and send padata at once; if it guessed wrong the KDC may return KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED without hints, and the client must retry with no padata.

Client and KDC both track five pieces of state during a request:

  • the reply key used to encrypt the KDC reply (conceptually a set of keys, starting from the principal's long-term keys);
  • how strongly the client's identity has been authenticated;
  • whether the reply key has been used;
  • whether the reply key has been replaced;
  • whether the client can verify the origin of the KDC reply.

Once the reply key has been replaced, knowing it no longer proves who the client is. A mechanism that sets a new reply key not based on the long-term secret must either verify the KDC reply another way or mark it unverified, and the client must return an error unless a later mechanism verifies it.

Clients may ignore padata they choose to, but must not ignore the padata defined in section 5.2 of the RFC. A KDC may ignore inappropriate padata, must ignore padata of unknown types, and must not ignore padata types it used in earlier messages. The KDC should not send data encrypted in the principal's password-based long-term key, since that has the same exposure as Kerberos without pre-authentication.
sections.eli5: Both sides keep a little scorecard: which key are we using, have we proved who you are, and can you be sure the answer really came from the right guard. The rules say how each step updates the scorecard.

sections.title: The Four Facilities and Mechanism Requirements
sections.content:
The RFC describes what mechanisms do as four conceptual facilities. A mechanism may offer one or several, and must meet the security requirements for each facility it offers.

  • Client Authentication proves the user's identity to the KDC before a ticket is issued, as the encrypted timestamp of RFC 4120 does. Such mechanisms should require the client to prove knowledge of the reply key before a successful reply is sent.
  • Strengthening Reply Key adds extra secrets to a weak, often password-based key, for example from a Diffie-Hellman exchange or a smart card. A mechanism that changes the key before it knows the other side understands it sends a proposal, and the other side accepts it.
  • Replace Reply Key swaps the key a successful AS reply is encrypted in. It must not be used if a man-in-the-middle is possible, and the reply key must then be marked replaced.
  • KDC Authentication verifies the reply came from the expected KDC even after the reply key was replaced.

Mechanism specifications must state each message's pa-type and contents, every change to the pre-authentication state, and which facilities they offer. Designers should protect cleartext parts of padata: by the end of a successful exchange, both sides must have verified all plaintext the other sent, and with more than one round trip, no message may have been reordered or replayed. Primitives from RFC 3961 are recommended for integrity and confidentiality, which keeps mechanisms crypto-agile.
sections.eli5: A pre-authentication step can do up to four jobs: prove who you are, make your secret key stronger, swap in a new key, or prove the guard is the real guard. Each job has its own safety rules.

sections.title: Cookies, Key Combining and Authentication Sets
sections.content:
KDCs are stateless, and a client may reach a different KDC for each message. So when more than one message is needed, the KDC hands the client an opaque cookie (PA-FX-COOKIE, type 133) that the client copies exactly into its next message. The contents are a local matter of the KDC, which is why KDC implementations from different vendors cannot generally be mixed in one realm. A KDC must include a cookie in KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_REQUIRED and KDC_ERR_MORE_PREAUTH_DATA_REQUIRED (91), and may end a conversation by omitting it. KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_EXPIRED (90) tells the client to restart.

When several mechanisms must all succeed, the KDC offers a PA-AUTHENTICATION-SET (134); the client picks one and echoes it in PA-AUTH-SET-SELECTED (135) using exactly the same octets. An unknown selection yields KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_BAD_AUTHENTICATION_SET (92).

To combine keys, KRB-FX-CF1 concatenates two passphrases, and KRB-FX-CF2 combines two protocol keys using the pseudo-random function PRF+ and exclusive-OR, with two distinct pepper strings so identical keys do not give a trivial result.

An optional AD-authentication-strength authorization element (70) lets a KDC record which mechanisms authenticated the client, so policy can distinguish strong from weak pre-authentication.
sections.eli5: The guard forgets you between visits, so he gives you a sealed note to bring back that reminds him where you were. When he wants several answers from you, he lists the sets of questions he will accept and you pick one.

sections.title: FAST: The Armored Channel
sections.content:
Kerberos is vulnerable to offline dictionary attacks: an attacker can request an AS reply and try passwords against it. FAST (PA-FX-FAST, type 136) reduces that exposure. FAST does not itself authenticate the client or the KDC; it provides an encrypted tunnel with typed holes for factors. When combined with encrypted challenge, an attacker needs a successful man-in-the-middle attack to observe ciphertext.

The tunnel uses an armor key, fresh for each conversation. The one armor type defined, FX_FAST_ARMOR_AP_REQUEST (1), carries an AP-REQ whose ticket is an armor ticket, usually a TGT. The key is KRB-FX-CF2(subkey, ticket_session_key, "subkeyarmor", "ticketarmor"), so both client and KDC contribute. The RFC prefers a TGT obtained with host keys, then anonymous PKINIT with a verifiable KDC (RFC 6112, RFC 4556), then anonymous PKINIT without KDC authentication, which is open to man-in-the-middle attacks when the armor TGT is obtained.

In a request, KrbFastArmoredReq holds the armor, a keyed checksum req-checksum binding it to the outer request, and the encrypted KrbFastReq with fast-options, the padata and a req-body that a conforming KDC uses in preference to the outer body. The hide-client-names option (bit 1) makes the KDC name the client as the anonymous principal in replies. Unknown critical options (bits 1 to 15) yield KDC_ERR_UNKNOWN_CRITICAL_FAST_OPTIONS (93).

The reply carries an encrypted KrbFastResponse with padata, an optional strengthen-key (required for a TGS reply), a finished structure with a ticket checksum, and the client's nonce, which the client must verify. Errors travel the same way, with a PA-FX-ERROR (137) item that holds the real KRB-ERROR.
sections.eli5: FAST is a locked tube between you and the guard. The lock key is made from a piece you choose and a piece the guard chooses, so nobody outside can read the questions or answers.

sections.title: The Encrypted Challenge FAST Factor
sections.content:
The one factor defined here, encrypted challenge (PA-ENCRYPTED-CHALLENGE, type 138), authenticates the client with its long-term key, much like the encrypted timestamp of RFC 4120. The client encrypts a timestamp in a challenge key made by KRB-FX-CF2 from the armor key and the long-term key. Because the armor key is fresh and random, so is the challenge key. A client may base its timestamp on the KDC time from an error, so it does not need synchronized clocks, but using the current time avoids letting an attacker make it appear to authenticate in the future.

The KDC decrypts the timestamp, returning KDC_ERR_PREAUTH_FAILED if that fails and KRB_APP_ERR_SKEW if the time is outside its clock skew. It should check for replays, but two challenges are a replay only if the ciphertext is identical, not merely the timestamp. If it accepts, it replies with its own encrypted time and must strengthen the reply key before issuing a ticket.

The factor provides Client Authentication and KDC Authentication and uses the strengthening facility, but not Replace Reply Key. Conforming implementations must support it.
sections.eli5: You write the time on a note and lock it with a key only you and the guard can make. If he can open it, he knows it is you, and his own locked note back proves he is the real guard.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC argues that encrypted challenge meets the requirements of the facilities it offers, and adds no unauthenticated cleartext. FAST optionally authenticates the KDC, but it is up to each FAST factor to authenticate the client. Factors must be bound to the conversation, ideally to the armor key, or a man-in-the-middle could cut and paste a factor between conversations.

Anonymous PKINIT armor does not always authenticate the KDC before the conversation begins. Tracking the KDC-verified state ensures the client has authenticated the KDC by the end, but designers must consider factors used before then. Mechanisms that checksum the request must checksum the inner request, not the outer one.

For the TGS exchange, the armor key must be tied to authenticating the client. The implicit TGS armor does this using the TGT sub-session key, and future TGS armor types must do the same or authenticate the client another way. A client should have a local policy that rejects replies lacking PA-FX-FAST-REPLY, and the RFC warns about downgrade attacks when falling back.
sections.eli5: The tube is only safe if every message is tied to this one visit. Otherwise a sneaky person could copy a note from another visit and slip it in.

sections.title: Constants and IANA Registries
sections.content:
The RFC lists constants first introduced here: errors 90 to 93, key usage numbers 50 to 55, authorization data elements 70 to 72 (AD-authentication-strength, AD-fx-fast-armor, AD-fx-fast-used), and padata types 133 to 138. It also creates IANA registries under Kerberos Parameters for pre-authentication and typed data, FAST armor types and FAST options.

Pre-authentication and typed data share one namespace, by convention with PA- or TD- prefixes. Registration needs expert review for mechanisms that authenticate users or KDCs or establish the reply key, and IETF review if the method is broader. FAST armor types and FAST options are assigned by standards action.
sections.eli5: Every special word in the system gets a number on a shared list, so two programs agree what each one means.

items.desc: Group of mechanisms that must all succeed.

items.desc: The authentication set the client chose.
